Pele Yoetz 50:3: And it is not fitting for a person to seek greatness, for they said (Pesachim 87b): rabbinic office buries its holders - for one cannot escape the great evil of pride except through strength, might, and a constant war [against it]. But it is fitting for every city to appoint over itself one leader to guide and lead them, and to be advised by his counsel. And they must be very careful of his honor and not defy his word - even if all are equal in stature, let them give greatness to one, that he be like a king over the troop. And likewise in every single household there shall be a head of the household, and the head shall take counsel from the younger, and the younger shall honor the head and not defy his word - for this is a great principle for the settlement of the world, the establishment of cities, and the peace of the home. For if people said, why should this one be made king over us and rule over us to put to death and to demolish and to abandon, and what advantage does he have over us - let us all be kings - the world would be destroyed. So too in every city and every household there must be one who is great and a leader; by his word they shall encamp and by his word they shall journey. Go forth and learn from the structure of the body, that the head is above - and if the feet said, why should the head be above, we too want to be above - the body would be inactive. Therefore not everyone shall be heads, but rather by common consent they shall appoint one head, and through this there shall be peace within their ranks, tranquility within their palaces.
Pele Yoetz 51:1: Fence - It is a mitzvah upon every single Jew to make a fence so as not to transgress the Torah, as it is written (Leviticus 18:30), "and you shall keep My charge." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Mo'ed Katan 5a): make a safeguard for My charge. And everything is according to what kind of person he is and according to how his inclination overpowers him - he must make a fence for himself and forbid to himself even the permitted, so as not to come to permit the forbidden. For example, one accustomed to excessive drinking shall forbid to himself every kind of drink, and if he needs to swear an oath and can uphold it, let him swear an oath, in the manner of what is written (Psalms 119:106), "I have sworn and I will fulfill it, to keep Your righteous judgments." Or let him make a fence for himself with a monetary penalty for every time he transgresses, or fence himself with a fast or some mortification and the like, as much as he can bear and not transgress. And the commentators have already written that although they said (Rambam, Hilchot De'ot 1:4) that a complete middle way is best, not to follow after excesses and prohibitions, and also not to be overly abstinent from the world nor overly righteous, and there is a limit to everything according to what kind of person he is - this applies to one who has not become accustomed to an evil way, but one who is accustomed to an evil way must distance himself from the ugly thing and its like to the very last extreme, until in time he can maintain the middle way and not depart from it. And the men of the Great Assembly already commanded us and made a fence for the Torah (Avot 1:1), and this is the Torah of man - the Torah of every single person is in his own hand, to make a fence for himself according to what he needs.
Pele Yoetz 51:2: And as for the great fence I would envision for the path of life, in order to turn away from asking [for what is improper], I have found only one good thing which I learned from our holy Torah, which said (Numbers 15:39), "and you shall see it and remember all the commandments of the LORD." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Menachot 43b): seeing leads to remembering, remembering leads to doing. If you do this thing and are able to sustain it, take a sheet of paper and write on it in this language: I hereby accept upon myself, without a vow, for a month's time, to read everything written here once every day, as a fixed practice, without fail - and if I transgress, I shall give a shekel of silver as a penalty to charity for every day. Son of man, son of man, remember your Creator; remember that you are a Jew; remember that there is good reward for the righteous and evil and bitter punishment for the wicked, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is exacting to the hair's breadth. Son of man, son of man, strengthen and exert yourself against your inclination, for whatever a man desires he can do. Run to a mitzvah and flee from transgression (Avot 4:2), and reward is according to the pain (ibid.). All of a man's labor is for his mouth (Ecclesiastes 6:7). Guard your mouth and your tongue from forbidden foods and doubtfully forbidden foods and from gross eating and from forbidden speech and even from idle words, for it is written (Malachi 2:17), "you have wearied the LORD with your words." "An abomination to the LORD is every proud heart" (Proverbs 16:5). Correspondingly, I [shall be] among the crushed - those who are insulted but do not insult, who hear their own disgrace and so on (Shabbat 88b, Yoma 23a, Gittin 36b) - I shall recognize my own small worth and limited understanding and the enormity of my sins, and I shall rejoice in afflictions and be clean, and my sin shall always be before me (Psalms 51:5). And through this we shall be saved from many evils - anger, dispute, and the like. "I have set the LORD always before me" (ibid. 16:8) - this is a great principle in the Torah. And I believe with complete faith that the whole earth is full of His glory - how then could my heart allow me to transgress the will of a high and exalted King, awesome and fearsome, and provoke Him to His face and do evil in His eyes, before Him?
Pele Yoetz 51:3: And let him take the great confession and see which transgressions he is accustomed to and habitually tramples upon, and let him record on this sheet: how can I do this great evil and that one, whose punishment is such and such, and why should I transgress this mitzvah and that one and that one - why should I not have mercy on my own soul, why should I not have mercy on my Maker's honor? Is it not better to have one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world than all the life of the World to Come, and one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come is better than all the life of this world (Avot 4:17)? Correspondingly, the distress of the soul in the World to Come, even for one hour, is worse and more distressing than all the evils of this world, and one hour in which a person provokes his Creator, a high and exalted King, is a greater distress and evil to those who fear the LORD and esteem His Name than the evils of the World to Come. Behold, therefore, I hereby accept upon myself, without a vow, to be careful of this and that, and to fulfill this and that, and if I transgress today any of these, I shall give a penalty for each thing, such and such, and as an atonement for my past sins I shall conduct myself with abstinence and mortify myself thus and so, without fail, and may the LORD God help me. Help us, God of our salvation, for the sake of the honor of Your Name, and so on. And on the following day let him see whether he stood guard, and if he transgressed, let him immediately set aside the penalty he stipulated, and let him repeat reading the text and add to it progressively, or reduce it, according to what he sees in himself that he needs and can sustain. So shall he do day after day and month after month, without fail - and if he can do this with a good friend, so that those who fear the LORD speak to one another, how good and how pleasant it is. Test me in this, and see wonders - for the writing is the writing of God, and the reading and remembering are a great fence, a stronghold and a tower (and I shall write more of this under the entry "Zechirah" [remembrance] and the entry "Sayag" [fence]) - provided he does not let a single day pass without doing this, all the days of his life, and behold, the LORD stands over him.
Pele Yoetz 52:1: Gentile - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yerushalmi Terumot, end of ch. 8) that one must be careful not to anger even a lowly gentile, for "you have transgressed a preserved matter forever," and their kingdoms follow their patrons [in the heavenly spheres]. And it is brought in the Yerushalmi regarding a swineherd whom the Jews struck, and who eventually became a king, and had it not been for Rabbi Yehoshua, who had done him a kindness, he would have wanted to bring destruction. And one must also be concerned, even if he cannot do anything, that he might find him alone in the dead of night or in the middle of the road, and that gentile with a band of his friends, and it could lead to danger. Behold, therefore, it is not good to quarrel with a gentile, even a lowly and disgraceful one, for you do not know what a day may bring, and it is found that he transgresses "and you shall greatly guard your souls" (Deuteronomy 4:15). And even if it merely brings a curse upon himself, that too is not good - for they said (Bava Kamma 93a, adapted): let not the curse of an ordinary person be light in your eyes, as we wrote above under the entry "Berachah" [blessing]. On the contrary, let him greet every person first with peace, even a gentile in the marketplace, and if the LORD has widened his boundary, "a man's gift makes room for him" - let him give gifts from time to time to gentiles, to fulfill what is said (Ecclesiastes 11:1): "cast your bread upon the waters, for you shall find it after many days." And it is especially necessary for men close to the government and to positions of authority to do kindness with all gentiles, for they have many enemies out of jealousy - their eyes grow dim at seeing a Jew in greatness and power - and even if he does them evil by the power of his own authority, "you have transgressed a preserved matter forever," and they shall take vengeance and bear a grudge like a serpent until his own day comes when his authority ends - for there is no person who does not have his hour. Of such a case it is said (Ecclesiastes 7:14): "on the day of good fortune, be in good spirits, but on the day of adversity, consider."
Pele Yoetz 52:2: And how shall a Jewish man ensure that everyone loves him, seeks his good, and stands by him in his time of need, if not by doing kindness and giving gifts freely to all gentiles - for a bribe blinds the eyes. And the sage already said: do not let a thousand thousand friends seem great in your eyes, nor let one enemy seem small in your eyes, for one enemy can kill a king. Therefore, whoever guards his soul shall seek peace with every gentile, small and great - and even if the gentile strikes him or curses him or robs him and the like, let him bow his head and bear it for the atonement of sins, for the LORD told him to curse - and at that very moment let him bless over the evil with great joy, and say: blessed is He who has not made me a gentile [i.e. subject to their harsh treatment without a countervailing law]. And I have already written above that God considered exile a good thing, and what the gentiles devour of Israel's substance, he shall consider it as charity, as it is written (Isaiah 60:17), "and your oppressors, righteousness" [i.e., that which oppresses shall be counted as charity]. And everything depends on what kind of person he is and on how much concern there is, even a remote concern - for certainly if we come to allow them to devour, and continue to devour, our money, "let whoever is hungry come and eat" - and what shall we eat? Rather, every clever person shall act with knowledge, fleeing from quarreling with a gentile as much as he can bear, and shall seek mercy from the LORD to save him from an evil man, and shall be a lover of peace and a pursuer of peace and shall increase friends - and through this we shall live among the gentiles until our Maker has mercy on us and breaks the exile from off our necks, and settles Israel securely upon our land and the inheritance of our fathers, so may it be His will, speedily in our days, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 53:1: Joy - It is written (Psalms 2:11): "rejoice with trembling." Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 30b): where there is joy, there shall be trembling. For it is the way of soldiers at war, when they see the enemy standing against them growing strong, that they too shout out and cry out loudly against their enemy to grow strong - so too, in a place of joy, a person's inclination grows strong against him, thinking: now he has fallen into my hand, for the fear of God is not before his eyes, and he is only occupied with celebrations and joy, and it entices him to forget the Rock of his salvation - then it shouts and cries out. But a fool multiplies forbidden words and forbidden sights and the like, various kinds of forbidden things that come about through excessive eating and drinking. Therefore the man who fears the LORD shall set the LORD before him always, and before he enters a place of joy shall accept upon himself not to go out of line in eating and drinking, and not to increase conversation and the like among the other prohibited things likely to come to his hand, and in the midst of the joy shall remember pure fear of the LORD - and this is a special property that the wine not harm him and drive him out of his senses. And it was already told about the master Rabbi Yisrael Ba'al Shem Tov, that once he drank a large cup of very strong beer, thinking it was wine, and he almost fainted, and immediately he closed his eyes for barely a moment and returned to his normal state as though he had not drunk at all. His students asked him what remedy he had used, and he answered them: do you not know what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Bava Batra 10a) - fear dispels the harshness of wine? And there is no fear like the fear of the LORD, adorned in His majesty - therefore, as soon as I thought deeply of the fear of the LORD, the intoxication passed from me. And then one must fulfill the mitzvah of remembering that which angered the Holy One, blessed be He, and the remembrance of Jerusalem - for in the manner they said (Beitzah 15b) regarding the verse "remember the Sabbath day" (Exodus 20:8), remember it precisely when there is cause to forget it (Beitzah, ibid.) - so too in this matter, the essential mitzvah of these remembrances is at times of celebrations and joy, which come to cause forgetfulness. And this too shall be a great fence, that he not go out of line but rather conduct himself in a straight way, by measure, by weight, and by measure of capacity.
Pele Yoetz 54:1: Body - Behold, the body compared to the soul is considered as nothing, and even less than vanity, and it is fitting for every person of understanding to afflict his own body, and to burden it with every kind of trouble in order to bring merit to his soul and give peace of mind to his Maker, and he shall not spare his body at all in a matter involving the honor of Heaven, but rather guard his body only so that it be healthy and strong to serve his service, the service of a servant. And our eyes see that every person is willing to suffer every kind of suffering in his money and his body, and this is his consolation, saying "a deduction from death" [a small loss counted against the fear of death], that the stroke of death not touch him - if he is so concerned about the departure of the soul from the body even though, if he lives many more years, a person must eventually die, all the more so should he be concerned about the separation of the soul from the body if he knew that he would walk before the LORD in the lands of the living. Rather, all there is to be concerned about is that through the union of the soul with the body, he can merit the path of life above and turn away from the depths of Sheol below. It is found that everything a person has, he should give for his own soul - body and money - just as he would give to avoid being killed, and this applies to every person.
Pele Yoetz 54:2: However, the man whom the LORD has graced with knowledge, to truly love the LORD as befits one who is a soul of the [divine] soul, shall also give his own soul for the sanctification of the Name, to the point that even if it were possible that one who serves the LORD would inherit Gehinnom and descend to the pit of destruction, and his soul would be burned and become ashes, for the sake of giving peace of mind to his Maker - such is our obligation and such is fitting and proper for us. But who is the wise man who shall understand this (Jeremiah 9:11)? In any case, let us do what is in our power to do, to a place our own hand can reach, and let us not spare our body for the sake of giving peace of mind to our Former, and may the LORD God help us, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 55:1: Shaving - Shaving is included in the honor of the Sabbath and festivals, that one not enter into them while unkempt. And according to the mystical secret of these matters, since hair represents an aspect of judgment, it is fitting to be very careful to shave every Sabbath eve, so as not to bring evil upon oneself by giving strangers power to rule over him, God forbid. And one must also be careful to shave before midday, for after midday is a time when the husk grows stronger, and therefore we have heard a warning to be exacting about this even on a Sabbath eve. And if a new moon falls on a Sabbath eve, let him shave earlier, on Thursday, for danger is more severe [than prohibition], and one must be concerned for the testament of Rabbeinu Yehudah HeChasid. And he shall be careful, when at the time of shaving hairs from his head fall upon him, to immediately shake them off. And in a place where there is a Jewish barber, he should not shave through a gentile, for the Kabbalists wrote that one who shaves through a gentile removes the image of God from himself. (And this is the reason I shave only once every fifteen days, to choose the lesser evil, even though there is a remedy - the heart hesitates.) And the remedy for this is to intend the Name of God in this manner: [a mystical formula], and to say before shaving, "and God created man in His own image, in the image of God He created him" (Genesis 1:27). And after shaving one must wash his hands.
Pele Yoetz 55:2: And from this you shall understand that it is not good what those do who grow the hair of their grown sons' heads for beauty and ornamentation, curling it - for besides transgressing "a man shall not wear a woman's garment" (Deuteronomy 22:5), also, according to the mystical secret of these matters, it appears that it is necessary for the hair of his head to fall to the ground, to remove the dominion of arrogance from him - except during the days of the Omer, when according to the mystical secret it is not fitting to shave from the eve of Passover until the eve of Shavuot. And it is fitting to conduct oneself thus in order to give peace of mind to our Former, only he should stipulate beforehand that it be without a vow - and so it is fitting to do regarding every good custom.
Pele Yoetz 55:3: And the disciples of the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote that at the time of shaving one should intend that he does not allow the rounding of the corners of his head or the destruction of the corners of his beard, in order to fulfill his Creator's warning, and through this it is considered as though he had fulfilled a negative commandment through a positive act. And I am accustomed to say, before shaving:
Pele Yoetz 55:4: For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, I am prepared to shave the hair of my head for the honor of the Sabbath, and I am prepared to be careful not to round the corners of my beard, to fulfill what the Torah said (Leviticus 19:27): "you shall not round the corners of your head, and you shall not destroy the corners of your beard" - vanity of vanities to everyone [i.e., all is done] to give peace of mind to our Former and to repair matters at their root in the supernal place. "And let there be favor," and so on. "And God created," and so on.
Pele Yoetz 55:5: And it is fitting for every God-fearing person that no blade touch his beard at all, neither on the face nor beneath the throat, for this causes great harm to his soul. And regarding the corners of the head, is it not good for every person to do as the master Ari, of blessed memory, held - that he leave [the hair] from the ear to the end of the temples, which is the place where the hair extends beyond the hairline of the forehead, and its measure is a little above the height of the ear? And why should not every person practice this piety and its like - what trouble is there and what monetary loss is there, and the matters are ancient and bear fruit above - why should he not have regard for his Maker's honor in a matter that costs him nothing? Therefore let every person make himself like a Torah scholar, and not worry about the mockers who say "sidelocks of a sage."
Pele Yoetz 55:6: And likewise, trimming the fingernails is part of the honor of the Sabbath, and one must be very careful to trim them every Sabbath eve - whether for the honor of the Sabbath or because if they grow somewhat long, to the point that one is bothered by them, they interpose for the washing of hands, and it is found that he recites the blessing over washing the hands and eats bread without a proper washing. And according to the mystical secret of these matters, since fingernails too represent an aspect of judgment, it is fitting to be very careful not to let either the fingernails or the toenails grow, for besides that it is good, when we immerse for purity, that the mitzvah be performed properly and we check ourselves for anything that interposes for immersion, like a woman purifying herself for her husband, moreover one must be very, very exacting to remove the grip of the husks from oneself - not as the common custom, which is concerned only about the fingernails. And it is good to be concerned not to cut them in their natural order, for although the master Ari, of blessed memory, mocked this practice, in any case he did not forbid it - and what does it matter to be concerned for the view of the Abudarham, who wrote that it is difficult [i.e., leads to a bad outcome, such as] burying children, may the Merciful One save us. And it is known, the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Niddah 17a): whoever burns them [nail clippings] is pious, whoever buries them is righteous, whoever scatters them is wicked.
Pele Yoetz 55:7: And especially must the woman who trims her nails for her own purification be careful. And one must also be careful not to cut them onto one's clothes or onto any garment. And ritual slaughterers, who must grow their nails long, and one who is a mourner, God forbid, must be careful to dig out the dirt beneath them and clean them each time, so that they not interpose for the washing of hands - and moreover, it is a disgraceful thing in the eyes of all who see it, and those who eat with them, if they see them putting their hand into the dish, their own soul is disgusted by the food and it becomes loathsome in their eyes. Therefore let every person be careful to be clean before the LORD and before Israel.
Pele Yoetz 56:1: Reciting Texts - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 63a): let a person recite [texts] first, and afterward understand [their reasoning]. And it is stated in the Talmud (Eruvin 48a) that Rav Pappa said: if I had not [first memorized through] recitation, I would not have [been able to] study analytically. Behold, therefore, it is not fitting for a Torah scholar to spend all his days in analytical study and dialectic sharpness alone, but rather he should set fixed times each day to study analytically according to his ability - Talmud or halachic authorities - and the rest of the day he should devote himself to studying broad proficiency in Talmud and halachic authorities (as shall be written below under the entry "Limud" [study]), in a manner that his hand be in everything and he be expert in all the laws. And especially since, instead of spending time on analysis and dialectic debate over the words of the later authorities, demolishing and building and writing about them on matters that have no practical halachic consequence, it is better that he occupy himself during those times with studying broad proficiency - to understand, become wise, listen, learn and teach, keep and do and fulfill.
Pele Yoetz 56:2: This is the teaching for a person who studies Torah for its own sake: all his study, even when he studies analytically and dialectically, should be through vocal recitation, for great is the virtue of the voice of Torah, and the letters fly upward, and everything ascends and builds his chambers in heaven. And whoever studies sitting alone and his hand [silent] loses much good (as written under the entry "Kol" [voice]). And if, while studying, it appears to him that there is an error in the book, he should not hasten to correct the book and change the reading - for many times a person is mistaken and thinks the book is in error, when in truth his own understanding is what errs, and we have heard a curse from the holy Rabbis that the hand which is excessive in correcting books shall be cut off, may the Merciful One save us - unless, after much analysis, it seems clearly to him that there is an error, in which case he performs a mitzvah by removing the obstacle, and he shall write in the margin of the book, "it appears that it should say thus." This is the straight path - "whatever is a glory to the one who performs it and a glory to him from men" (Avot 2:1, Nedarim 22b).
Pele Yoetz 57:1: Rebuke - Rebuke is necessary, to rebuke transgressors if they understand, since "a rebuke enters more deeply into a person of understanding" (Proverbs 17:10). But it is better to speak in a gentle tongue, for "a gentle tongue breaks a bone" (ibid. 25:15). And rebuke draws anger for the one who rebukes and dispute and quarrel from the one rebuked, for not every person accepts rebuke - and especially nowadays, even small children do not accept much rebuke from their father and mother. Therefore this is the straight path: that the one who admonishes choose to speak in a gentle tongue and a sweet, smooth palate, and not speak harshly, but rather let his palate be full of sweetness - and especially if it is in the presence of others and in public, he should not rebuke his fellow, for it is found that he shames his fellow's face in public, of which our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 3:11) that he has no share in the World to Come. Therefore one must be very careful of this. And especially in the synagogue, where there is also the matter of the honor and reverence due to the synagogue, it is forbidden to rebuke - and even if he sees his fellow committing an idolatrous act [i.e., something as severe], God forbid, he should not raise his voice with force to rebuke him, for he injures his own soul, and this is like one who washes his clothes facing the sun - the clothes become white while he himself becomes black. And this is the hint of the ashes of the red heifer, which defile the pure and purify the impure - so too this one seeks to correct his fellow while he himself becomes corrupted. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already explained (Arachin 16b) on the verse (Leviticus 19:17), "you shall surely rebuke your fellow and not bear sin because of him" - that a condition of the mitzvah of rebuke is that one not shame him and not bear sin. Therefore, if he wishes to keep him from a prohibition, let him go to his fellow and speak his words to him privately, with pleasant speech, or wait until he finds him alone and rebuke him to his face in a fitting manner, according to what kind of person he is and the need of the hour, and always speak in a low voice with soft speech, for this indicates humility and submission, as it is written (Isaiah 29:4), "and you shall be brought low, you shall speak from the ground, and your speech shall be humbled from the dust." And "the voice of fools is in a multitude of foolish rebukes" - a matter of confusion to the listeners, confounding and misleading them - but the words of the wise, heard in calm, are pleasant and accepted by the listeners.
Pele Yoetz 58:1: Letter Dalet: Cleaving - Cleaving to the Name, blessed be He, is one of the 613 mitzvot: that one cleave to the Name constantly with great desire, with sparks of the flame of love, and there is no better trait than this, for everything is within it - and according to its importance, so is the difficulty of attaining it. Everything depends on a person's own deeds and on his efforts in thought, speech, and deed - it grows day by day, and one who sanctifies himself below is sanctified from above (Yoma 39a), until a spirit from on high is poured upon him and purifies and sanctifies him. And every person is obligated, according to his own measure, to strive with all his strength to fulfill this mitzvah and its like at every time he remembers. And how good it is that it be written for him in the place where he sits, to be a remembrance between his eyes always. And whoever comes to purify himself is helped [from Heaven] (Shabbat 104a, Yoma 38b).
Pele Yoetz 58:2: And behold, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Ketubot 111b) on the verse (Deuteronomy 11:22), "and to cleave to Him" - is it possible for a person to cleave to the Shechinah? Is it not written (ibid. 4:24), "for the LORD your God is a consuming fire"? Rather, cleave to His attributes - just as He is merciful, so shall you be merciful; just as He is gracious, so shall you be gracious (Shabbat 133b). And every person imagines that he is already cleaving to His attributes, blessed be He, for all Israel are merciful, sons of the merciful, and there is no person who does not show grace to the poor - but to be truly like Him, blessed be He, one must have mercy and show grace even to his enemy who seeks his harm, and even if he is an evildoer who stands and defies him, he should not withhold his goodness, mercy, and kindness from him - even if that very kindness he receives shall be used against him for evil - nevertheless he should not withhold his goodness from him, just as the Holy One, blessed be He, conducts Himself with His creatures. And the holy master Rabbi Moshe Cordovero has already gone to great lengths in the book Tomer Devorah to explain the thirteen attributes of mercy and how every person should conduct himself according to them, and I, the poor one, have copied a summary of his words in the pamphlet "Orot Elim" (page 155). Happy is the man who listens to have these thirteen attributes read to him at least once a month, and who strives with all his strength to act according to this order - with the help of the Almighty he shall ascend, and he too shall be able to be likened to the One on high.
Pele Yoetz 58:3: And further, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Ketubot 111b): whoever cleaves to the wise is as though he cleaves to the Shechinah. And greater than this they said (Berachot 64a): whoever benefits from a feast in which a Torah scholar dwells is as though he benefits from the splendor of the Shechinah. (However, this is not said of everyone who is called by the name "Torah scholar" nowadays, for exposition is not the essential thing but rather the deed - Doeg and Achitophel and Jeroboam were great sages and were driven out of this world and the World to Come, and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Bava Batra 4a) that "you shall not curse a prince among your people" (Exodus 22:27) applies to one who does the deeds of your people.) And the sage to whom one must cleave is one whose fear of sin precedes his wisdom, and whose deeds exceed his wisdom, and for whoever sits with him or reclines with him at a meal, his mouth opens in wisdom and teaching of kindness is on his tongue, and all his words are words of Torah and the way of life, and words of ethical rebuke - and even the ordinary conversation of Torah scholars requires study (Sukkah 21b, Avodah Zarah 19b), for even what appears at first glance to be idle conversation, one who examines it finds good sense and knowledge in it, for he wished to teach a person knowledge or the wonders of the LORD's kindnesses and the like, and all his words are for the sake of Heaven, in a manner that whoever cleaves to him constantly shall in the end learn from him and walk in the way of life, and shall be guarded in the paths of the righteous. And of this our Sages, of blessed memory, warned, saying (Berachot 28b): keep your children from idle logic-chopping and seat them between the knees of Torah scholars. And the Tanna taught (Avot 1:4): let your house be a meeting place for the wise, and warm yourself before the fire of the sages, and cover yourself in the dust of their feet, and drink in their words thirstily.
Pele Yoetz 58:4: And it is known that such is the craft of the evil inclination, that it always sits at a person's right hand to accuse him and distance him from every good thing, and all the more so from this matter, since it knows this shall be its undoing - for they said (Sukkah 52b): if this scoundrel confronts you, drag him to the study house; if he is like stone, he shall melt, if he is like iron, he shall shatter. And it is written (Deuteronomy 32:2), "my teaching shall drip like rain" - for just as rain pierces the stone, so too one who goes constantly to the study house and hears words of Torah and words of ethics and fear of the LORD, these pierce the heart of stone, and a steadfast spirit is renewed within him. Therefore the evil inclination arranges that if a person goes once to the study house and sits there an hour or two, his soul shall become disgusted with it, and he shall prefer instead to go to a place of frivolity or sit all day and all night with idlers, without becoming tired or weary - on the contrary, he shall find rest and peace of mind there. And of this the Holy One, blessed be He, complained: "you have not called upon Me, O Jacob, for you have grown weary of Me, O Israel" (Isaiah 43:22). But the man who is pure and has removed the veil of blindness from his eyes knows for certain that in order to be a worthy Jew serving God, he must overcome his inclination - and it is enough for this that he overcome his inclination to study or hear teachings constantly, even against his own will and to his own displeasure, and in the end it shall become sweet and pleasant to him, and he shall go on growing and advancing in the ways of unity, abstinence, and piety - as stated, that the special property of Torah is to burn away the impure spirit, and therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, said (Yerushalmi Chagigah 1:7): would that they had forsaken Me and kept My Torah, for the light within it would bring them back to the good. And "he who walks with the wise shall become wise" and shall attain the paths of life - therefore, do this and live.
Pele Yoetz 59:1: Road - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yerushalmi Berachot 4:4): all roads are presumed dangerous. And it is known, their saying, of blessed memory (Shabbat 32a), that a person should not enter a place of danger, for perhaps no miracle shall be performed for him, and if a miracle is performed for him, they deduct from his merits. And the greatest evil found on the roads is that one cannot serve the LORD a complete service and be careful of all prohibitions, and therefore they said (Psalms 84:5): "happy are those who dwell in Your house" - for many evils befall travelers, who live a life of hardship, [suffering] heat by day and cold by night, and the master and his attendant strike them, and many such afflictions. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Gittin 70a) that travel shortens a person's days and years, as it is said (Psalms 102:24), "He afflicted my strength on the road, He shortened my days." And all the more so those who wander from place to place and city to city to gather money - their evil is great, for after all the toil and trouble there are places where their gift [in charity] is small and their disgrace is great, and there are places whose community is poor and can barely pay the travel expenses, having no means to give further charity to the poor man - and if they do give, it is a small amount. It is found that the community's expense is great while the poor man receives only a small amount, with shame, disgrace, and much dishonor. And sometimes, after the poor man has gone about weeping for several years, leaving his wife and children lying in hunger, in the end robbers or thieves plunder him, and the poor man returns home empty-handed, full of sorrow and sighing, doubled and redoubled grief - and would that even his own life not be touched, that he not become a corpse in the ground, God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 59:2: Therefore, whoever has a brain in his skull should not go on such roads unless he has already acquired a reputation there such that a brief journey can gather much, sufficient for his need - but otherwise, all who go regret it, and mostly these travelers are embittered in soul, with no intention of returning home, but rather going from misfortune to misfortune, may the Merciful One save us; may the good LORD atone for them.
Pele Yoetz 59:3: And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Ketubot 68a): we presume goodness even toward a swindler [regarding claims of poverty]. But certainly there are also found good men who have the trouble of daughters who have come of age, and many such necessary and unavoidable household expenses, and the poor man has nothing - what shall that man do, where shall he turn for help if not to go on the roads to seek relief, especially in these times when dowries and the expenses of daughters have multiplied? Certainly toward such men it is fitting to have mercy and help them with every kind of beneficial assistance, and it shall be counted a great mitzvah. But the trouble is that we are suspicious of swindlers, and they already bring letters of testimony to holy men in the land, to tell their trouble and distress to the many - but what benefit is there in giving such a letter of praise for the bearer, when it increases everyone's distress and no one checks into it to know the truth about him, and therefore people do not rely on or pay attention to such letters, and treat all faces alike. And therefore the modest ones withdraw their hands from giving a letter to anyone, for they are concerned about testifying falsely, and if they cannot avoid it, they write within the letter a hint alluding to what kind of person the bearer is, and that they gave him this letter only under necessity. And for one whom they truly know deserves mercy, they write differently, so that the listener shall hear and understand from the letter whether to draw near or keep away. This is the straight path. And in any case, whoever can avoid going on the roads, whether to gather funds or for business, happy is he and happy is his portion - happy is he in this world and it is well with him in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 59:4: Therefore it is good for a man to be self-restrained and it shall be good for him, and to sit in his own house - "better a dry morsel with tranquility in it" - sitting in his house, dependent on his own table, and serving his Maker, he and his children with him. However, if it is decreed upon him from Heaven that he must go on the roads, and he cannot avoid it and must go, let him do this: let him first pray for his own trouble, and before setting out on the road let him perform an order of farewell, and let charity go before him and set his footsteps on the road. And every single day he should not fail to say the Traveler's Prayer as established by our Sages, of blessed memory (Berachot 29b).
Pele Yoetz 59:5: And it is especially necessary to be careful on the road with mitzvot, such as prayer, tzitzit, and tefillin, and he should not worry about the mockery of gentiles to the point of neglecting a mitzvah - heaven forbid to do this. And one must guard against a prohibition, whether light or severe, and conduct himself with piety in whatever comes to his hand while traveling on the road, since all roads are presumed dangerous, and with what shall he gird himself with strength to be saved if not with Torah and good deeds, which are like a shield against calamity? And it is true that it is difficult to be careful and diligent on the roads, but the hour requires this - to be diligent and press oneself as much as possible - and of such a case we say: whatever is in your power to do, do. And how good it would be for him to strive greatly to fulfill the words of the Sages, who said (Pesachim 2a): let a person always leave in good light and enter in good light. And it follows naturally that he shall pray properly at the inn, for one who prays on the road prays a short and rushed prayer. And it is known, the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Berachot 14a), that whoever prays and then sets out on the road, the Holy One, blessed be He, fulfills his needs. Therefore, if he sets out on the road after midday, let him first pray Minchah at home, and it is also very good to enter [an inn] early, and its owner shall live [prosper], and many times a road has proven fatal because one was not careful about this. And especially on the eve of the Sabbath he must be very, very careful to rest while it is still broad daylight, and "prepare what you shall bring" (Exodus 16:5) for the Sabbath. And how good and how pleasant it is if his lips move with words of Torah by heart - sound wisdom shall guard him, and the verse is written (Deuteronomy 6:7): "and you shall speak of them when you walk on the road." And one accustomed to the Holy Zohar shall see with his own eyes the virtue of one who walks on the road and studies - no evil shall befall him, for the angel of the LORD encamps around him. Of this it is said (Psalms 119:1): "happy are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the LORD."
Pele Yoetz 60:1: Proper Conduct - The branches and details of proper conduct are many. The teaching of proper conduct is longer than the earth [an idiom for vast extent] - is it not written in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, Tractate Derech Eretz? And further, it is explained in the books of the masters of ethics, such as the holy book "Reshit Chokhmah" at its end, and the book "Shnei Luchot HaBrit," and the book "Shevet Musar" (ch. 16), in the testaments attributed to Rabbi Eliezer the Great. Whoever is a man who desires life shall search thoroughly to keep the way of the tree of life, for truly they said (Vayikra Rabbah 9:3) that proper conduct preceded the Torah. And especially one who is in the category of a Torah scholar - if he has no proper conduct, he desecrates the Name of the LORD and the Torah. And we learned (Avot 3:10): whoever the spirit of creatures is pleased with, the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased with him. And this is a great principle in proper conduct: that he do the good and the upright in the eyes of God and man, and set aside his own will for the will of others, and let his mind be in harmony with people's minds. And in whatever a person learns of the laws of proper conduct, he has not discharged his obligation until he becomes wise and understanding of his own mind, for these are matters that have no fixed measure - everything depends on the place, the time, and what kind of person he is; one must conduct himself with each person according to his own character, and fathom his mind and do his will as his will, if it is not against the Creator's will.
Pele Yoetz 60:2: And one must always love the word "perhaps" (Sefer Chasidim 95) and be concerned lest he burden his fellow. Therefore how precious are the words of King Solomon, peace be upon him, who said (Proverbs 25:17): "let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house" - for sometimes a person thinks he is honoring his fellow and goes and sits with him for several hours, not knowing what is in his fellow's heart, who thinks: when will you leave, for I have much business and you are delaying me. And sometimes words become more burdensome than a heavy load, whether because they are slanderous words like a madman scattering firebrands, or because he prolongs his words excessively, or because he inquires and investigates matters beyond him, and many such things. Therefore every clever person shall act with knowledge, and his words shall be pleasant to hear and few, so that people not grow weary of them - and even preachers must be careful not to prolong their trouble, but rather say a little of good, and let the listener listen. And it is better that they say of him, how brief he is, than that they say, how long-winded he is. And nowadays brevity in everything is a sharp coin current in this age, and they say, in a manner of elegance, "and he said to the reapers, the LORD be with you" (Ruth 2:4).
Pele Yoetz 60:3: And likewise one should not burden a person with the sight of his own eyes. If he wishes to do something in secret, such as a mitzvah or charity and the like, you too should keep it secret so that he not be distressed by your seeing it, and what you saw, do not tell, and act as though you did not know. And likewise, if you saw your fellow with new items, act as though you did not know they were new. We learned (Ketubot 17a): Beit Hillel say, "a beautiful and graceful bride" [regardless of her actual appearance]. From here we learned not to disparage a purchase your fellow has already made, but rather to praise it in his presence - and all the more so if he is pleased that someone else bought it for him, for if you disparage it in his presence, or tell him "I bought a better one more cheaply" and the like, it is like distress to his soul, and the one who bought it for him would be angry unto death, and hatred and rivalry would increase.
Pele Yoetz 60:4: One who asks his fellow for some kindness must be very careful not to burden him, and especially not to bring many friends along until he grants his request. And if he is an important man for whom it is embarrassing to send someone away empty-handed, one must be very careful not to ask anyone for anything for oneself - for besides that he becomes disgusted, there is also an element of theft if he does it against his will and to his disadvantage, as explained in Sefer Chasidim (316).
Pele Yoetz 60:5: King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 25:7): "it is better that he say to you, come up here, than that he put you lower in the presence of a prince." And he also said (ibid. verse 6): "and do not stand in the place of great men." A person should always sit lower than what seems to him his proper place, and should not go up in rank until they press him to the point of embarrassment. And the halachic authorities have already explained (see Pesachim 86b, Tosafot s.v. "ein") that in a matter of greatness and honor, one demurs even to a great man. And always honor every person slightly more than what seems to him fitting to honor him, for what does it cost a person to give extra honor, and if his fellow's spirit is thereby put at ease, it shall be counted a mitzvah for him - and especially guests and Torah scholars, he should honor them more than necessary, for he thereby performs an act of kindness. And how good it is to address everyone greater than oneself in wisdom or in years in the second person plural [a respectful form] and as "sir." And we learned (Avot 4:1): who is honored? He who honors [other] people. And since proper conduct fitting for each person according to his own character has already been treated in the books mentioned above, they have left me no room to elaborate on this - and further, it has already been stated that not every person and not every occasion are alike, and understanding is needed to fathom each person's own mind and do his will as his will, for there is a way that seems straight to a man, thinking to find favor in people's eyes, yet people's spirit is not pleased with him. Therefore one must inquire and search with wisdom and listen to counsel to know which is the straight path, and seek mercy from the Master of Heaven that He set him right with good counsel, to do the good and the upright in the eyes of God and man, and to find favor and good sense in the eyes of God and man, and let all his deeds be for the sake of Heaven, and the LORD shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence - "grace and honor the LORD shall give" (Psalms 84:12).
Pele Yoetz 61:1: Knowledge - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 33a): whoever has no knowledge, it is forbidden to have mercy on him. And they further said (Vayikra Rabbah 1:15): whoever has no knowledge, a carcass is better than he. And they further said (Berachot 33a): whoever has knowledge, it is as though the Temple were built in his days. And they further said (ibid.): great is knowledge, for they placed it as the first blessing among the intermediate blessings [of the Amidah]. And they further said (Vayikra Rabbah 1:6, Tanchuma Vayikra 1): if you lack knowledge, what have you acquired, and if you have acquired knowledge, what do you lack? And truly, all unity [with God] and all human perfection and all the good of this world and the World to Come depend on knowledge, and this applies to every person.
Pele Yoetz 61:2: And certainly the reason they were severe in punishment and condemnation of one who has no knowledge is regarding one who could have learned knowledge but, because of his laziness and pride and following his own inclination, did not learn knowledge. And the "knowledge" spoken of here is not knowledge of dialectic wisdom, for exposition is not the essential thing but rather the deed (Avot 1:17) - rather, knowledge is needed to know how to conduct oneself in a straight way through Torah as befits a Jewish man, and to conduct oneself with good traits and uprightness, in peace and equity with every person, and to accept everything with joy and a good heart, and to be happy with one's portion, and to conduct oneself with proper conduct, and to do the good and the upright in the eyes of God and man - for so upright intellect and knowledge require. And truly they said (Sotah 3a): a person does not sin unless a spirit of folly enters him.
Pele Yoetz 61:3: And the greatest knowledge that is needed is to recognize in oneself that one has no knowledge, and to always seek to learn knowledge from every person, and all the more so from one who is greater than oneself in wisdom and in years, from whom one must learn knowledge - or a person shall learn from books and from the mouths of scholars which is the straight path, and even if his own mind does not agree with theirs, he shall nullify his own opinion before theirs, and believe with complete faith that if there is an emptiness, it is in himself, because of his own limited knowledge and deficient understanding, for "wisdom is with the aged, and understanding is length of days" (Job 12:12). And this is the evil of man upon the earth, that he is wise in his own eyes and the way of a man is upright in his own eyes. Therefore, in this let the wise man glory in his wisdom - when he becomes wise enough to recognize that he has no knowledge, and when he recognizes that he does not recognize his own deficiency. And the sage already said (see the Treasury of Parables and Proverbs): I have no certain knowledge except what I know, that I do not know. And the sage said (ibid.): I did not know that I knew, until I knew that I did not know. And therefore Solomon said in his wisdom (Ecclesiastes 1:18): "he who increases knowledge increases pain" - for he increasingly recognizes his own deficiency, lowliness, and poverty. And this applies to matters of Heaven, but in worldly matters, "he who increases knowledge" shall attain "gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away" (Isaiah 35:10) - for according to upright knowledge, there is no room to be distressed or exacting or angry about anything in the world, and whoever has acquired knowledge seems as though he lacks nothing, as though he had the whole earth and its fullness, for all is vanity and vexation of spirit, and whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good (Berachot 60b) (and more is written in the pamphlet "Beit Tefillah" in the blessing "Atah Chonen").
Pele Yoetz 61:4: And since everything depends on knowledge, one must be very diligent to acquire knowledge by listening to counsel and studying books and hearing teachings. And this shall be a sign in his hand: when he knows that he knows nothing, then he shall know that he has acquired true knowledge. And for this let every pious person pray before the God who graces man with knowledge, that He graciously grant him wisdom and knowledge, in order to know the way we should walk and the deeds we should do, as required, without deficiency. And knowledge is also needed regarding money matters and guarding the body, for it is written (Proverbs 24:4), "and by knowledge the rooms are filled," and it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:12), "and wisdom preserves the life of those who have it." And although it is written (ibid. 9:11), "bread does not come to the wise," and it is written (Proverbs 30:22), "a fool when he is filled with bread" - the explanation of this and the like is that there are three kinds of decrees. Sometimes it is decreed upon a person specifically that he be wealthy - of him it is said (I Samuel 2:7), "He also exalts," meaning that the Holy One, blessed be He, exalts him even against his own will. And likewise if it is decreed upon him that he be alive and healthy - then, if he passes through water, it shall not sweep him away, and if he walks through fire, he shall not be burned. But if it is decreed upon him that he be poor, or that he shall die, or that he be crushed with afflictions - if he labors with schemes and knowledge, all his labor shall be in vain and he cannot annul the decree of Heaven, for the needy shall not cease. And if he guards his body, he shall watch in vain, and he cannot annul the decree of the One who dwells on high, for the hope of man is doomed.
Pele Yoetz 61:5: However, there are cases where it is decreed from Heaven that a person shall have life, peace, and wealth according to nature, according to his own sharpness and effort and according to his own care and conduct - therefore one must be concerned that perhaps His wisdom, blessed be He, has decreed thus, to give to a man according to his own knowledge and toil. Therefore let a person go out to his craft and his labor, and consider carefully, according to his own knowledge, which way holds the light to bring sustenance to his household and preserve his health, and the LORD too shall give the good - but on condition that he not neglect his Maker's service for the sake of his money, and not labor to grow rich through forbidden means, and not neglect Torah study in order to guard his body with excessive care - for this the LORD certainly did not command, and it is a culpable matter that prevents the good, and is like one who extinguishes a fire with straw, which only increases the flame.
Pele Yoetz 61:6: And all that has been said on this matter applies to one who does not do the will of the One who dwells in the heights and must conduct himself according to the manner of proper conduct, and to one who makes his occupation permanent, who is given over to nature. But the man who fears the LORD, whose desire is in the Torah of the LORD and who greatly desires His mitzvot, and who makes his Torah study permanent and his occupation occasional, the LORD shall command a blessing with him beyond the natural order, and his body shall be healthy and strong with mighty strength - even though sufferings and toil and trouble increase, "those who hope in the LORD shall renew their strength," wealth and riches shall be in their houses without deficiency, whether by knowledge or without knowledge. And this is the explanation of the verse (Proverbs 16:20): "he who deals wisely in a matter shall find good, and whoever trusts in the LORD, happy is he" - meaning that he does not deal wisely in the matter at all, but rather trusts in the LORD - happy is he.
Pele Yoetz 62:1: Speech - Much speech is harsh, and little of it is pleasant. And I said, let me gather all kinds of speech, whose general categories are three: mitzvah, permitted, forbidden - and their details are many, and I shall explain them so that they be a remembrance between the eyes of the man who fears the LORD. Before he speaks any word, let him clarify its category - if it is a matter of mitzvah or of the permitted, without any hint of prohibition, let him speak; but if there is any hint of prohibition, let the man tremble and be seized, and be like one mute, not opening his mouth, for all of a man's labor is for his mouth (Ecclesiastes 6:7). And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Kohelet Rabbah 6:6) that all the evil of man in the World to Come is because of what he sins with his mouth. And they further said (Vayikra Rabbah 4:2) that all the mitzvot and good deeds he performs and all his labor in Torah shall not suffice against what he sins with his mouth. (And more is written on this below under the entries "Peh" [mouth] and "Sichah" [conversation], but such is my way, to return to a subject.)
